rationale: The imaging analysis compares cortical thickness in prodromal and established Lewy body and Alzheimer dementia. Hallucinations enter the clinical definition and symptom context. Imaging groups and figure labels do not provide a dried fig exposure or an episode-rate comparison.

The report follows a Parkinson case with Capgras misidentification after bilateral subthalamic stimulation. The authors discuss perioperative and clinical contributors. Capgras delusion and postoperative course are distinct from a dietary comparison of visual hallucination frequency.

The experiments use cerebrospinal-fluid exosomes from Parkinson, Lewy body dementia and comparator groups to examine alpha-synuclein effects and aggregation in cell assays. Figure references identify laboratory results. No fruit is administered or compared.

A clinical account of lesion-associated peduncular hallucinosis with REM sleep behavior disorder is paired with functional connectivity analysis. The visual experiences occur in the setting of a focal lesion. There is no dried fig comparison or ingredient-linked episode result.

The Parkinson mild cognitive impairment study classified 12 patients without visual hallucinations and nine with them, with 19 controls. It compared FDG uptake and later cognitive outcomes. Dementia progression was observed in both Parkinson subgroups. The data stratify existing hallucination status without assigning food.

The clinician-rated Parkinson psychosis scale evaluates hallucinations and delusions, including individual features such as frequency and disruption. The validation reports inter-rater agreement and drug-response examples. Its measurements describe psychosis assessment and provide no dried fig comparison.

The archive compares cardiac MIBG SPECT/CT and planar imaging in clinical diagnostic groups including Lewy body diseases. Visual hallucinations inform diagnostic context. The figures depict scans and sympathetic imaging rather than fig exposure.

The study compares visual perceptual organization in autopsy-verified Lewy body and Alzheimer dementia. Visual task performance is an experimental measure distinct from spontaneous hallucination episodes. No exposure to dried figs is assigned.

Parkinson participants with and without hallucinations and healthy controls completed a visual perception threshold task. Functional imaging compares brain activity around conscious detection. Existing visual hallucination questionnaires and task measurements are separate from a food exposure.

The paper follows a Parkinson transplant case with extensive graft survival and restored dopaminergic innervation, yet limited sustained motor benefit. Motor scores, graft histology and figure references describe the procedure. There is no tested fig intake or after-food symptom contrast.

The investigators compare reported hallucination characteristics in Parkinson disease and schizophrenia. The instrument distinguishes reported frequency, perceived properties and disruption across sensory modalities. These are diagnosed-group comparisons without a fig exposure.
The study compares depression and clinical symptom items in Lewy body and Alzheimer dementia. Depression ratings and hallucination history are distinct. No dried fig intervention is studied.

Two Parkinson case reports consider focal nonmotor seizures as a differential for recurrent episodic changes. The clinical descriptions distinguish transient alterations from overlapping Parkinson nonmotor symptoms. There is no visual episode rate under fig ingestion.

Parkinson patients underwent cognitive rehabilitation or a control activity in a longitudinal study. Outcomes include functional and cognitive tests with brain imaging. Fig labels identify illustrations. No courses of dried fig intake or resulting visual episode counts were compared.

The Parkinson cohort compares subjective cognitive complaints with objective neuropsychological performance. Exclusions and clinical covariates define the cohort. It does not estimate hallucination frequency after fig exposure.

This post hoc rotigotine comparison tabulates participants with adverse events across older and younger groups. Visual hallucination adverse event entries and clinical imaging or figures do not count episodes under dried fig intake.

The 360-degree Picture Interpretation Test compares executive measurements in Parkinson disease and controls. Detection and interpretation of a depicted scene are not spontaneous hallucination episodes. No dietary fig exposure is included.

The case discusses visual hallucinations as a diagnostic clue in corticobasal syndrome with amyloid imaging and an alternative Lewy body explanation. The observed course and imaging are a differential diagnosis, without dietary exposure or a measured after-fig change.

The Parkinson online study measures object-recognition performance and records the presence or absence of visual hallucinations. Recognition task impairment and binary symptom presence do not measure spontaneous episode rates under dietary fig exposure.

The imaging study compares functional network dynamics among Parkinson cognitive groups and healthy controls. The reported states reflect neuroimaging time series. No culinary fig intervention or after-food visual hallucination frequency outcome is reported.

In pooled Parkinson dyskinesia trials, 18 participants assigned extended-release amantadine and three assigned placebo reported visual hallucinations. Nine of the 18 amantadine reports began within the first 30 days. These are people with drug adverse events and time to first occurrence, without episode frequency per person or a fig exposure.

The study compares EEG-derived network measurements in Lewy body dementia, Alzheimer dementia and controls. Neuropsychiatric symptoms help describe clinical groups. Signal frequency bands and past symptom status are distinct from hallucination episodes under a diet.

The study follows lower urinary tract outcomes in male Parkinson patients receiving istradefylline. It records one participant with a mild visual hallucination adverse event. This is a drug follow-up event without a dried fig exposure or repeated episode counts.

The study compares hippocampal subfield volumes across Parkinson psychosis groups and controls. Visual hallucinations and minor phenomena help define clinical groups. Imaging comparisons do not estimate an episode-frequency change under fig exposure.

The investigators map lesions associated with parkinsonism to a shared functional network and compare it with stimulation targets. The study addresses causes of lesion-associated motor symptoms. It does not investigate a dried fig or hallucination-frequency exposure contrast.

The cross-sectional comparison estimates sex ratios in Lewy body dementia, Parkinson dementia and Alzheimer disease. Visual hallucinations are discussed as diagnostic features. There is no food-exposure or episode-frequency comparison.

The retrospective series follows 28 people with advanced Parkinson disease using waking-day apomorphine pumps. It compares impulsive-compulsive behaviors around changes in dopamine agonist treatment, with no dried fig exposure or separate episode-rate comparison for visual hallucinations.

The two-year Parkinson follow-up asked 78 people about feeling of presence and hallucinations. Seventeen developed a new feeling of presence, seven of them developed subsequent hallucinations, and 26 developed first visual hallucinations. The study measures onset and sequence rather than within-person episode frequency under a fig exposure.

The 20-item self-report validation separates visual misperceptions, sensory experiences and other psychosis phenomena. The paper records instrument construction and comparison with clinical assessments. It does not assign dried figs or estimate their effect on visual episodes.

The case series describes three advanced Parkinson patients on intestinal levodopa-carbidopa gel with dyskinesia and high body temperature during a heatwave. Acute mental-state changes and environmental triggers are discussed. There is no fig exposure or clinical hallucination frequency comparison.

The pilot protocol plans a computerized intervention for motor slowing and motor fatigue. It excludes participants with visual hallucinations. The eligibility field provides no measured hallucinations or food comparison.

The investigators compare brain proteins HSP90 and two co-chaperones in Parkinson and Lewy body dementia tissue. The methods and figures are neuropathological. They do not contain an assigned fig preparation or clinical visual episode measurements.

The clinical registry analysis uses factor analysis of histories and neurological findings from 165 patients seen in an early neurodegenerative-disease clinic. The clusters describe groups of symptoms. No dried fig intervention, dietary association or individualized visual episode rate was investigated.

The study compares resting MEG oscillatory power between Parkinson patients with visual-only, multimodal or absent hallucinations. Frequency of neural oscillations and reported visual episode frequency are separate concepts. No fig preparation was administered.

The case uses FDG-PET patterns to support a clinical Lewy body dementia diagnosis. Perceptual symptoms enter the diagnostic discussion. Figures are images and do not represent a fig exposure or dietary episode outcome.

The study examines the pathology of a PSEN1 variant carrier, including Alzheimer and diffuse Lewy body changes. Figures depict immunohistochemistry. It reports no dried fig intervention or measured Parkinson visual episode rate.

Participants with Parkinson disease and controls underwent flicker exposure to test whether it elicits visual experiences. The study did not reliably reproduce participants' everyday hallucinations. Elicited phenomena under optical stimulation are distinct from spontaneous episodes after dried figs.

The retrospective cohort includes 25 people with Lewy body dementia and 31 with Alzheimer disease. Presentation and timing of survival-related complications differ by diagnosis. The source discusses clinical hallucination presence without assigning or evaluating a fig exposure.

The retrospective comparison follows medication discontinuation and safety in Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia psychosis. It documents composite reasons for discontinuation and symptom improvement in clinical records. There is no dried fig comparison or prospectively counted visual episode rate.

The case links severe ocular hypertension to endocrine disease and later treatment, with visual aura and other symptoms recorded in the presentation. Ocular findings and suspected parkinsonism do not establish a fig exposure or Parkinson hallucination outcome.

The study compares perceptual task errors and response times in Parkinson groups with and without self-reported hallucinations and uses a smaller resting-state fMRI subset. Visual recognition errors, time variability and existing hallucination severity are separate from food-induced changes.

The experiments compare visually judged time intervals in Parkinson disease and healthy controls, with medication and stimulation conditions. The diagrams depict timing tasks. No dried fig or visual hallucination episode intervention appears.

Three cases describe chorea or a progressive supranuclear palsy-like syndrome following cardiac surgery and circulatory arrest. The clinical time course documents serious postoperative changes. There is no fruit intervention or assessment of Parkinson hallucination frequency under food.

The inherited hypermanganesemia and dystonia case describes psychosis and a course after oral iron. The physiological context and treatment are distinct from Parkinson disease and dried fig exposure. It supplies no food-attributed rate of visual episodes.
